# Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents

Mingze Yin Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Tencent
Affiliation: Equal Contribution    Xiaohan Wang Affiliation: Tencent
Affiliation: Equal Contribution    Dian Li Affiliation: Tencent   
Longfei Luo Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Zhongguancun
Academy    Jiahong Yan Affiliation: Tencent    Yiheng Zhu Affiliation:
Zhongguancun Academy    Chang-Yu Hsieh Affiliation: Zhejiang University
Affiliation: Corresponding Author

###### Abstract

While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable
capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in
isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from
historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing
self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction
trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured
behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore,
as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic
evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively
managing situational experience. To address this, we propose
Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that
systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive
evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically
grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation,
Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System
that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into
dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational
experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive
perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement.
Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework
compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual
curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that
Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a
controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric
adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.

###### keywords

Self-Evolving Agent, Agentic Skills, Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning

## 1 Introduction

By interacting with complex and dynamic environments, large language
model (LLM) agents have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a
broad spectrum of sophisticated tasks, including web navigation, vibe
coding, healthcare monitoring, and deep research \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\].
However, agents such as OpenClaw typically operate in isolation, lacking
the ability to learn from prior successes and failures. In particular,
users’ stable preferences and operational requirements, which are
gradually clarified through repeated interactions, remain restricted to
the current session and are not transformed into reusable experience for
environment awareness and autonomous evolution.

Therefore, self-evolving agent systems have recently emerged as a
prominent research direction, aiming to leverage recurrent interaction
experience through internal learning loops to support continual,
user-centric adaptation and refinement. Most existing self-evolution
paradigms directly use contrasted user interaction trajectories as
conditioning signals to distill long-term memory or overwrite practical
skills. However, indiscriminately injecting heterogeneous experiences
without explicit attribution into designated modules can not only
obscure the agent’s behavioral patterns, but also introduce substantial
challenges to update controllability. The absence of effective
mechanisms for controlled updating further compromises both the
stability of the evolutionary trajectory and the validity of the
acquired updates. Furthermore, as large language models continue to
improve in reasoning and planning, and as external tool libraries become
increasingly comprehensive, the relative contribution and marginal
utility of cognitive and behavioral experience may diminish
substantially. Under this trend, a core challenge for self-evolving
agents is no longer merely how to accumulate generic experience, but
rather how to systematically model, dynamically store, and efficiently
retrieve situational experience, thereby enabling rapid self-evolution
and effective adaptation to specific user environments.

It is not the strongest of the species that survives, nor the most
intelligent; it is the one most adaptable to environmental change. —
Charles Darwin

Inspired by this, we turn to the idea of accumulating
environment-adaptive experience to facilitate agentic self-evolution. We
propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive agentic self-evolving
framework that automatically distills episodic experience to drive the
comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory.

Theoretically, the agentic self-evolution is grounded in the iterative
co-adaptation between agent-actor trajectories and evolver-critic
trajectories. Darwin-Claw views self-evolution not as parameter update
in isolation, but as a closed-loop process in which interaction failures
are first attributed, abstracted, and consolidated into implicit
environment prototypes, and are then transformed into structured
experience that supports both immediate behavioral correction and
long-horizon capability growth. Specifically, the proposed Hierarchical
Experience Consolidation System extracts fine-grained error attributions
from user interaction trajectories and generalizes them into dynamically
updated prototype vectors that organize situational experience across
diverse environments. Built on this substrate, Experience-Driven Agentic
Holistic Evolution treats consolidated situational experience as
interaction patches for improving context-sensitive perception, while
distilling operational experience into explicit optimization signals for
external skills. Moreover, once environment-specific experience becomes
sufficiently accumulated and refined, it can be elevated into a dreaming
condition that further reshapes the agent’s long-term memory.
Darwin-Claw establishes a principled theory of self-evolving agents in
which situational experience serves as the core medium linking
environmental adaptation, skill refinement, and memory formation.

Practically, Darwin-Claw is designed as a general, environment-adaptive
evolutionary framework that is compatible with a wide range of
mainstream agent systems, incorporating OpenClaw, Claude-Code, Codex,
and Hermes. Specifically, experience consolidation driven by runtime
interaction without manual curation or explicit user intervention.
Hierarchical experiential attribution supports efficient vector
retrieval from a locally stored experience pool to enhance perception.
Episodic experience-driven memory distillation and skill updates are
generated through open-ended reasoning eliminating reliance on
predefined rules. Furthermore, experimental results on WildClawBench
demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial improvements across
tasks, highlighting the effectiveness of stable and efficient
self-evolution for building continuously improving agent systems in
real-world scenarios.

The primary contributions of this paper are as follows:

(i) Environment-adaptive agentic evolution. Hierarchical experience
consolidation system is constructed to attribute and accumulate situated
experience from users’ historical interaction trajectories, further
dynamically driving reusable optimization of both agentic memory and
skills.

(ii) Readily deployable agentic system. Darwin-Claw not only enables the
optimization of agent’s perception of specific interactive environments
via a skill-plugin mechanism, but also supports the collective evolution
of the skill ecosystem across multiple users.

(iii) Controllable evolutionary pathway evaluation. The comprehensive
validation of experience knowledge accumulation and execution strategy
optimization identifies a controllable pathway for agent self-evolution.
Multiple agentic benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of stable
evolution for task completion performance.

## 2 Method

We propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive experience-driven
agentic self-evolving framework. Darwin-Claw leverages the iterative
interplay between agent actor trajectories and evolver critic
trajectories to enhance the agent’s perception of diverse user
interaction environments, while further driving stable self-evolution
through contextual experience. Hierarchical Experience Consolidation
System (Section.
[2.2.1](#S2.SS2.SSS1 "2.2.1 Experience Consolidation and Knowledge Refinement ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Agentic Holistic Evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents"))
extracts error attributions from user interaction trajectories and
further generalizes them into implicitly updated environment prototype
vectors, which are then used to categorize and consolidate situational
experience. Experience-Driven Agentic Holistic Evolution (Section.
[2.2.2](#S2.SS2.SSS2 "2.2.2 Causal Validation and Multi-Dimensional Scoring ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Agentic Holistic Evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents")
and
[2.2.3](#S2.SS2.SSS3 "2.2.3 Externalized Memory Management and Evolutionary Lifecycle ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Agentic Holistic Evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents"))
leverages situational experience as interaction patches that can be
directly provided to the agent to improve perceptual responses, while
distilled operational experience is used to explicitly optimize external
skills. Once experience related to specific environmental factors has
been sufficiently accumulated and refined, it can further serve as a
dreaming condition to influence the agent’s long-term memory.

### 2.1 Problem Definition

We consider an agent $`\mathcal{A}`$ operating in an interactive
environment $`\mathcal{W}`$. Task-oriented interaction trajectories
$`\mathcal{T}=\{\tau_{1},...,\tau_{k}\}`$ are comprehensively collected,
including the user’s query, the agent’s actions, feedback from the
environment or the user, and the final task solution.
$`\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},...,s_{n}\}`$ represents the collection of
reusable procedural artifact skills preloaded into the agent under the
current interactive environment. The general agentic memory system is
simplified as $`\mathcal{M}=\{m_{s},m_{l}\}`$, where the short-term and
long-term memory are maintained separately. The algorithm aims to
extract reusable environment-aware experience $`\mathcal{E}`$ from
historical interactions, thereby comprehensively promoting agentic
self-evolution endowed with both memory mechanisms and operative skills.

````math
\mathcal{A}^{(t+1)}=\Psi\Big(\mathcal{A}^{(t)},\mathcal{E}\mid\mathcal{W}\Big)=\Psi\Big(\mathcal{A}^{(t)},\Phi(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{M}\mid\mathcal{W})\mid\mathcal{W}\Big)

### 2.2 Experience-Driven Agentic Holistic Evolution

#### 2.2.1 Experience Consolidation and Knowledge Refinement

As illustrated in Figure
[1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Method ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents")
Evolver Critic Pipeline operates asynchronously to process session
interactive logs and recursively accumulate situational experience to
further drive agentic self-evolution. The constructed experience
consolidation procedure consists of two complementary stages:

Phase 1: User Interaction Trajectory Parsing. To minimize computational
overhead, the system incrementally processes only new session traces
generated since the last evolution cycle. It parses the raw trace
$`\tau`$ to identify Skill Invocations (SIs)—complete segments
encompassing skill reading, tool execution, and observation. This is a
purely structural formatting operation without semantic intervention.

Phase 2: Experience Extraction via LLM Triage. Analyzing all traces is
computationally prohibitive. The LLM acts as a filter to determine
whether a trace contains learnable behavioral or perceptual patterns
(e.g., error recovery, tool substitution, repetitive retries, or
efficiency bottlenecks). Routine or flawless executions are particularly
discarded. Additionally, For traces exhibiting strong learning signals,
the LLM generates a structured Experience Unit (EU). Each EU
encapsulates specific trigger conditions, keywords, and actionable
handling strategies (categorized into exploit or explore subtypes).

#### 2.2.2 Causal Validation and Multi-Dimensional Scoring

To ensure the reliability of the externalized policy, we introduce a
rigorous validation mechanism for deploying generated episodic
experiences, grounded in principles of causal inference.

Causal Attribution: When a new EU is tentatively applied, a two-step LLM
pipeline evaluates subsequent traces. It first determines the relevance
(whether the new trace hits the EU’s context). More importantly, it
performs causal attribution: it assesses whether the observed change in
the agent’s performance is a direct causal result of reading the EU, or
merely coincidental.

Multi-Dimensional Scoring: The quality of each validated EU is
quantified using a weighted composite score based on three dimensions:
(i) Coverage ($`c`$): The hit rate of the EU’s keywords in actual
execution traces. (ii) Effect ($`e`$): The delta in task completion
rate. (iii) Efficiency ($`\eta`$): The reduction in invalid tool calls.

Evaluation score is defined as $`S=w_{1}e+w_{2}c+w_{3}\eta`$, where the
weights reflect our design philosophy: effect as the primary objective,
coverage as the prerequisite, and efficiency acts as a bonus factor.

#### 2.2.3 Externalized Memory Management and Evolutionary Lifecycle

Validated patches are deployed by writing EUs as inline blocks directly
into the corresponding SKILL.md files. To preserve prompt quality and
prevent performance degradation caused by information overload, the
system adopts a lifecycle evolutionary management mechanism.
Specifically, each skill is subject to strict slot limits (e.g., six
active slots, divided into three exploit and three explore slots) to
control context complexity. Within this framework, each EU progresses
through a state-machine lifecycle: new patches first enter a
probationary Nursery with limited capacity and a Time-To-Live (TTL),
where they must accumulate positive evidence ($`e>0`$) to be promoted;
promoted EUs then occupy regular Active slots, where they are retained
or replaced through competitive selection based on performance; finally,
EUs that consistently produce negative effects ($`e<0`$) or exceed their
TTL are automatically evicted and archived, while users may also
manually pin or evict specific EUs. Through this competitive,
experience-driven evolutionary process, the framework ensures that the
agent’s externalized memory preserves only the most valuable and
causally effective strategies, thereby enabling recursively holistic
self-evolution without modifying the underlying model parameters.

## 3 Experiments

We first evaluate on WildClawBench \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] whether skill
self-evolution can consistently improve task scores across diverse
real-world scenarios, spanning code intelligence, search and retrieval,
creative synthesis, productivity workflows, safety alignment, and social
interaction (Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Skill-Driven Holistic Self-Evolving ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents")).
We then evaluate the proposed skill self-evolution approach on the
iterative auto-research LLM optimization tasks based on RSIBench
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\], with a particular focus on whether it offers
significant advantages in the efficiency and stability of experiential
learning (Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Agentic Improvements in Application Scenarios ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents")).

### 3.1 Setups

Benchmark Suite. To evaluate breadth, we include WildClawBench
\[[6](#bib.bib6)\], which comprises 60 human-authored, long-horizon
multimodal tasks. The benchmark spans six thematic categories, including
Code Intelligence ($`12`$, $`20.0\%`$), Search & Retrieval ($`11`$,
$`18.3\%`$), Creative Synthesis ($`11`$, $`18.3\%`$), Productivity Flow
($`10`$, $`16.7\%`$), Safety Alignment ($`10`$, $`16.7\%`$), and Social
Interaction ($`6`$, $`10.0\%`$). On average, each task requires
approximately 8 minutes to complete and involves more than 20 tool
invocations. To evaluate depth, we incorporate RSIBench
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\] to investigate iterative improvements to
Qwen3-3.5-35B-A3B through customized Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) data
strategies. Holding the post-training stack fixed, the agent continually
accumulates empirical evidence to refine the SFT data strategy for
subsequent post-training rounds. The updated LLM is holistically
evaluated on SWE-bench Verified \[[8](#bib.bib8)\], SWE-bench
Multilingual \[[9](#bib.bib9)\], SWE-bench Pro \[[10](#bib.bib10)\],
GPQA Diamond \[[11](#bib.bib11)\], AIME 2026 \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], and
Terminal-Bench 2.0 \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], covering a broad spectrum of
capabilities, including software engineering, terminal use, science
question answering, and mathematics problem solving.

##### Agent Configuration.

Our evaluation comprehensively examines three widely adopted agent
harness frameworks paired with proprietary backbone LLMs: OpenClaw with
GPT-5.5 \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]; Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5
\[[15](#bib.bib15)\] and Claude Opus 4.8 \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]; and Codex
with GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.6 Sol \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. All agents
apply the same official model API, standardized task format, data usage
constraints, and computational budget, ensuring that observed
performance differences faithfully reflect the skill evolution effects.

##### Evaluation Protocol.

In RSIBench-Data, the agent iteratively proposes data strategies and
training configurations from a predefined whitelist. The target model,
optimization backend, serving interface, and evaluator remain fixed
across all runs. Candidate checkpoints are evaluated through the
benchmark-provided sandboxed service. In WildClawBench, each task is
executed from an identical initial workspace in an isolated Docker
container, using the native agent harness and real tools. Ground-truth
and grading-only assets are introduced only after the agent process
terminates. Timed-out runs are scored based on the artifacts and
environment state available at termination. Throughout evaluation, we
preserve complete interaction trajectories, tool calls, generated
artifacts, execution logs, and resource usage, ensuring evaluation
reflects reproducible end-to-end agent behavior beyond final-answer
scores.

Table 1: Self-evolving agentic performance across diverse real-world
tasks. The progress bar depicts the temporal improvement in the agent’s
task success rate as experience accumulates.

In this section, we conduct holistic analyses to reveal the detailed
task distribution of the agentic benchmark, demonstrate the performance
advantages of Darwin-Claw across diverse real-world application
scenarios, and provide quantitative analyses of adaptive experience
accumulation and skill expansion in dynamic environments. Concretely, we
evaluate GPT-5.5 under the OpenClaw harness on the diverse
human-authored, bilingual, and multimodal tasks in WildClawBench
\[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. As presented in Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Skill-Driven Holistic Self-Evolving ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents"),
Darwin-Claw demonstrates consistently superior performance over the
baseline across all evaluation dimensions. In terms of average score,
Darwin-Claw achieves substantial gains in overall performance
($`+24.1\%`$), with particularly strong improvements on web tasks
($`+27.3\%`$), tool-use tasks ($`+31.6\%`$), reasoning-intensive tasks
($`+22.7\%`$), and long-horizon tasks ($`+23.8\%`$). This advantage also
remains robust across increasing levels of task difficulty: the success
rate improves by $`+18.5\%`$ on easy tasks, $`+23.6\%`$ on medium tasks,
$`+29.4\%`$ on hard tasks, and $`+33.2\%`$ on extreme tasks. These
results indicate that Darwin-Claw generalizes effectively to
heterogeneous real-world scenarios requiring compositional
decision-making, cross-domain adaptability, and sustained execution over
extended interaction horizons. Moreover, the ablation study further
confirms the importance of each core component, as removing hierarchical
consolidation, prototype memory, or dual usage all leads to clear
performance degradation relative to the full model. Taken together,
these findings demonstrate that Darwin-Claw effectively transforms
episodic interactions into structured situational experience, yielding
more controllable, stable, and continual adaptation in realistic
multi-task agent environments.

We evaluated the data-driven auto-research application from
RSIBench-Data \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], primarily based on the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
base model \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] with post-training enhancement via
supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The agent leverages a fixed technology
stack to select data filtering strategies and training hyperparameters
for each optimization round, and can autonomously decide when to
terminate the optimization. We adopted two widely used harnesses, Claude
Code and Codex, paired with powerful closed-source models including
Claude Opus-4.8, Claude Sonnet-5, GPT-5.6-terra, and GPT-5.6-sol.
Previous methods mainly rely on offline large language models to extract
structured reports, which are then passed to the agent as references for
iterative training optimization. In contrast, our approach achieves
self-optimizing iteration of the agent’s capabilities in specific
scenarios through experience deposition and skill insertion. As shown in
Table
[2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Agentic Improvements in Application Scenarios ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents"),
the proposed skill-based evolving approach successfully uncovers better
post-training performance than the base model in 19 of 24 agentic
auto-research tasks. In particular, our method achieves absolute
performance gains of 32.00, 15.28, and 15.08 percentage points over the
original base model on SWE-V, AIME, and Terminal-Bench 2.0,
respectively. Moreover, skill-based evolving approach consistently
outperforms context-passing evolving approach across all six benchmarks,
increasing average performance from 28.42% to 31.91%. Notably, the
proposed method avoids the performance degradation observed with context
passing on GPQA Diamond. The relative gains are particularly pronounced
on SWE-P and Terminal-Bench 2.0, where average performance improves by
68.8% and 34.1%, respectively. Experimental findings suggest that
continually accumulating operational experience to improve skills is
particularly effective for tasks requiring complex procedural reasoning
and tool interaction. The solid self-improvement observed in the
auto-research scenario further demonstrates that distilling feedback
from each iteration into the continually enriched skill experience
provides an effective and reusable mechanism for adaptation.

## 4 Related Work

### 4.1 LLM-based Agent Systems

LLM-based agents combine reasoning, planning, memory, and tool use to
solve complex tasks through iterative interaction. ReAct
\[[19](#bib.bib19)\] established the widely adopted paradigm of
interleaving reasoning with executable actions. Toolformer
\[[20](#bib.bib20)\] and ToolLLM \[[21](#bib.bib21)\] further enabled
LLMs to select and invoke external APIs, while Reflexion
\[[22](#bib.bib22)\] and Voyager \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] introduced
feedback-driven improvement and the accumulation of reusable behaviors.
Complementary multi-agent frameworks, including AutoGen
\[[24](#bib.bib24)\] and MetaGPT \[[25](#bib.bib25)\], coordinate
specialized agents through role assignment and structured communication.
DSPy \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] instead provides declarative abstractions for
composing and optimizing LLM programs. These approaches primarily
optimize model interactions, execution policies, or agent workflows.
Reusable capabilities are typically represented as prompts, traces, code
snippets, or framework-specific modules, with limited support for
independent versioning, evaluation, distribution, and maintenance.

### 4.2 Self-Evolving of Agentic Skills

Skill-based self-evolution converts accumulated experience into reusable
and actionable behavioral abstractions. Trace2Skill
\[[27](#bib.bib27)\], AutoSkill \[[28](#bib.bib28)\], and SkillX
\[[29](#bib.bib29)\] derive transferable skills from execution traces
and organize them into extensible skill libraries, allowing agents to
reuse procedural knowledge without replaying complete trajectories.
Since automatically induced skills may be redundant, brittle, or
unreliable beyond their original tasks, closed-loop approaches such as
CoEvoSkills \[[30](#bib.bib30)\], Memento-Skills \[[31](#bib.bib31)\],
and SkillForge \[[32](#bib.bib32)\] couple skill generation with
verification and deployment feedback to iteratively improve skill
correctness, generality, and controllability. Extending this paradigm
beyond private agent adaptation, SkillClaw \[[33](#bib.bib33)\] and
EvoSkill \[[34](#bib.bib34)\] investigate population-level evolution
over shared skill repositories, where validation, admission, versioning,
and rollback are essential for maintaining the quality of collectively
accumulated capabilities. Additionally, SkillRL \[[35](#bib.bib35)\],
D2Skill \[[36](#bib.bib36)\], and XSkill \[[37](#bib.bib37)\] integrate
automatic skill discovery with reinforcement learning, utility
estimation, and hierarchical control, thereby enabling agents to jointly
improve reusable procedures and policies. Agentic skill self-evolving
holds considerable promise as a foundational paradigm for building
autonomous agents, enabling them to continually expand and refine the
behavioral capabilities.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving
framework designed to overcome the limitations of isolated and static
LLM agents. To address the challenge of effectively accumulating and
utilizing situational experience, we proposed a Hierarchical Experience
Consolidation System that systematically attributes interaction failures
and abstracts them into dynamic environment prototypes. Building upon
this substrate, our Experience-Driven Agentic Holistic Evolution
mechanism translates these consolidated experiences into actionable
updates, driving the continuous refinement of both external operational
skills and durable long-term memory. Practically, Darwin-Claw serves as
a readily deployable system compatible with mainstream agent
architectures, enabling not only personalized environmental perception
but also the collective evolution of skill ecosystems across multiple
users. Extensive evaluations on WildClawBench demonstrate that our
framework significantly enhances task completion performance.
Ultimately, Darwin-Claw establishes a principled and controllable
pathway for the continuous, user-centric evolution of autonomous agents
in complex, dynamic environments.
````
